Psychology: sport and performance

Concentration, pressure, motivation and teamwork.

What it does

Sport psychology studies the psychological factors that influence sport and performance, and how sport in turn influences health and well-being. It works with elite athletes, but also with children starting out, older people who exercise and other areas where people must perform under pressure, such as music, surgery or emergency services.

Where it works

  • Clubs, federations and high-performance centres.
  • Sports schools and grassroots sport, with coaches and families.
  • Injury rehabilitation and retirement from sport.
  • Physical activity programmes for health.

What works according to research

  • Setting goals about process (what to do) as well as outcome (what to achieve).
  • Pre-performance routines, like those before a free throw or a serve, which help focus attention.
  • Imagery: mentally rehearsing a movement improves its execution, especially when combined with real practice.
  • Self-talk that is instructional or motivational, rather than self-critical.
  • Motivational climate focused on learning and improving, which is associated with more enjoyment and less dropout among young people.

An example

In 1898 Norman Triplett observed that cyclists rode faster when competing against others than when racing alone against the clock, and tested it with children winding fishing reels. It is considered one of the first experiments in social and sport psychology. Today we know that the presence of others improves performance on well-learned tasks but can impair it on new ones.

Mental health in sport

Athletes such as the gymnast Simone Biles and the tennis player Naomi Osaka have spoken publicly about anxiety and depression. Their testimony has helped federations and the International Olympic Committee include mental health in athlete care, and not just performance.

References

  1. Triplett, N. (1898). The dynamogenic factors in pacemaking and competition. American Journal of Psychology, 9(4), 507–533.
  2. Weinberg, R. S. y Gould, D. (2023). Foundations of Sport and Exercise Psychology (8.ª ed.). Champaign: Human Kinetics.
  3. Reardon, C. L. et al. (2019). Mental health in elite athletes: International Olympic Committee consensus statement. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 53(11), 667–699.
  4. Hatzigeorgiadis, A., Zourbanos, N., Galanis, E. y Theodorakis, Y. (2011). Self-talk and sports performance: A meta-analysis. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 6(4), 348–356.
